chunks: Process node sizes and what 3nm means. The question: What are node sizes? What does "3nm process" refer to? Are transistors really that small?
A process node such as "3 nm" names a generation of chip manufacturing technology. Today the number is a marketing label. It is not the size of any part of a transistor.
A smaller number means a newer generation, which packs more transistors into the same area and generally uses power more efficiently.
Think of a "half-ton" pickup truck. The name once meant it carried about half a ton. Today it is just a size class.
A chip node name works the same way: it once matched a real length, and now it only says "this generation".
Unlike the truck name, a newer node does give a real gain, just not the one the number suggests.
If the names were literal linear dimensions, going from 28 nm to 3 nm would yield an 87 times density gain. An assumed 1. 7 times per generation gives 14 times .
The real gains from public foundry claims are somewhere in the lower curve's neighbourhood; the exact multiple is vendor-specific and not what the name implies. The 1.
7 times is an illustrative assumption, not a measurement.
Transistor: a tiny electronic switch. A modern chip has billions. Nanometer (nm): one billionth of a meter.
Process node: a named generation of chip manufacturing, such as "5 nm" or "3 nm". Transistor density: how many transistors fit in one square millimeter.
Pitch: the center-to-center spacing of repeated features, such as neighboring wires. Die: one chip's worth of silicon cut from a wafer.
If the names were literal lengths, shrinking from 5 nm to 3 nm would shrink each feature to 3/5 of its size. Area would shrink to (3/5)², so density would rise by (5/3)² about 2.
8 times . Real gains claimed by chip factories (foundries) per generation are closer to 1. 6 to 1. 8 times .
Real dimensions are also larger than the name: roughly 45 to 50 nm between neighboring transistors' gates (the part that switches it on and off), and about 20 to 30 nm between the tightest wires.
These are estimates. Some thin layers inside a transistor really are only a few nanometers thick, but the spacings that set density are ten times larger. That is the whole idea.
"A node name like 3 nm used to mean a real feature size, such as gate length or half-pitch, but since roughly the 2000 seconds it's a marketing label for a generation.

Real dimensions on a '3 nm' process are tens of nanometres, a contacted gate pitch around 45 to 50 nm and metal pitch about 20 to 30 nm, though a few features like fin or sheet thickness are a few nanometres.
Density gains per node are about 1. 6 to 1. 8 times , not the 2. 8 times the name would imply. Transistors are 3D now: FinFETs and gate-all-around, patterned with EUV."
